notes: Youth segregation judicial review; PSO 4950/1700 interaction and pre-decision representations are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Young offender segregation: PSO regime and right to be heard

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: SP, a 17-year-old sentenced young offender at New Hall, was segregated under YOI Rule 49 between 25 September and 15 October 2003 for good order and discipline after threats involving razor blades.
She sought declaratory relief that segregation breached PSO 4950 chapter 7 purposeful-activity requirements and that she was denied an opportunity to make representations before segregation.
The Secretary of State accepted she did not receive the chapter 7 hours of activity but argued PSO 1700 permitted a curtailed segregation regime.
The initial segregation order was made about 24 hours after SP told a CARATS worker she wanted to harm others with a razor blade.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with permission on two grounds relating to prison segregation of a child in a young offenders institution.
enrichment.outcome: First claim dismissed: combined PSO 4950 and PSO 1700 did not require full chapter 7 regime in segregation; second claim upheld in principle that fairness required an opportunity to make representations before initial segregation unless good order, discipline or urgency justified proceeding without it.
enrichment.ratio: PSO 4950 chapter 7 applies to segregated young women but only to the extent consistent with PSO 1700 part B paragraph 4.1.1; mentioning an exclusivity or tie-up agreement is not a breach of confidentiality under PSO terms. In the post-HRA context for a vulnerable child, fairness generally requires pre-segregation representations unless security, good order or urgency prevents it, notwithstanding R v Hague on post-decision safeguards.
legal_issues: Whether segregated under-18s must receive PSO 4950 chapter 7 purposeful activity hours
How PSO 4950 and PSO 1700 interact for Rule 45/49 segregation
Whether a segregated inmate must be allowed representations before the initial segregation decision
Whether YOI Rules or Prison Rules governed SP at New Hall

notes: Short youth court reopening judgment; functus officio and autrefois acquit point is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Youth court could not reopen dismissed indecent assault charge
key_facts: A 17-year-old faced an indecent assault charge in Stratford Youth Court; prosecution witnesses failed to attend on 19 January and 24 March 2004.
On 24 March the justices refused an adjournment, the Crown offered no evidence, and the charge was dismissed.
Minutes later the complainant arrived and the court reconvened, abandoning section 142 and purporting to reopen under an inherent power.
The CPS later confirmed the complainant had left the jurisdiction and no retrial was possible even if the review failed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a youth court decision to reopen and adjourn proceedings after dismissal following no evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; the justices' decision to reopen proceedings after dismissal was quashed.
enrichment.ratio: Once the prosecution has offered no evidence and the court has dismissed the charge, the magistrates are functus officio; any further prosecution would give rise to autrefois acquit and the court has no power to reopen the case on that basis.
legal_issues: Whether a magistrates' court may reopen a case after offering no evidence and dismissal
Scope of section 142 Magistrates' Courts Act 1980
Whether an inherent power to reopen exists in the interests of justice

confidence.notes: Short judgment with a single clear holding. Retrial impossibility is noted but not central to the legal conclusion.

notes: Detailed guidance on Education Act 1996 ss 316/316A and Schedule 27 paragraph 3; remitted for rehearing.

enrichment.short_title: Mainstream schooling duty for children with special educational needs

statutes_considered.title: Special Educational Needs and Disability Act 2001

key_facts: D, a 12-year-old with emotional and behavioural difficulties, had a statement of special educational needs maintained by Hounslow LEA.
His mother preferred mainstream school C but the LEA specified special school S; the SEND Tribunal upheld the LEA.
Pitchford J allowed a reasons challenge and gave general guidance on sections 316 and 316A, which the Court of Appeal reviewed on second appeal.
The parties accepted the LEA need not trawl every mainstream school but disputed how particular schools should be considered after paragraph 3 rejection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal giving guidance on the meaning of sections 316 and 316A after remittal to a differently constituted SEND Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Guidance varied from Pitchford J: section 316 does not impose a duty to name a particular mainstream school but normally the LEA/Tribunal should exercise discretion to do so; late parental nominations in the section 316 process are not re-tested under paragraph 3(3) suitability criteria.
enrichment.ratio: The paragraph 3 Schedule 27 process (parental preference for a named school) is distinct from the section 316 process (mainstream placement duty). Section 316 creates no mandatory duty to name a school in Part 4, but authorities should normally name one; when considering particular mainstream candidates after lawful paragraph 3 rejection, suitability under paragraph 3(3)(a) does not reapply and all nominated schools are considered equally under section 316 criteria.
legal_issues: Whether section 316 requires naming a particular mainstream school in a statement
Relationship between Schedule 27 paragraph 3 and sections 316/316A
Whether suitability remains relevant when considering alternative mainstream schools on appeal
Effect of Richardson v Solihull after the 2001 Act amendments

notes: Convictions quashed after PII hearing but detailed reasons reserved in a confidential judgment; public transcript is procedural.

enrichment.short_title: Kassar drug importation convictions quashed for disclosure failure
key_facts: Mr Kassar was convicted in July 1993 at Newcastle Crown Court of two counts of fraudulent evasion of prohibition on importing cocaine and sentenced to 24 years.
The Criminal Cases Review Commission referred the case in March 2003 citing prosecution disclosure failures regarding Customs and Excise material about Mr Asare's role.
At a PII directions hearing the court examined undisclosed material in chambers; the prosecution then declined to contest the appeal.
The appellant chose not to attend the hearing from Long Lartin prison.
enrichment.procedural_posture: CCRC reference under section 9 Criminal Appeal Act 1995 following a PII hearing on undisclosed prosecution material.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and convictions quashed; fuller reasons to be given in a confidential judgment for the prosecution only.
enrichment.ratio: Where undisclosed Customs and Excise material relevant to assessing Mr Asare's role was never assessed by trial counsel or the judge, and Asare was central to the prosecution case, the appeal must succeed for disclosure failure.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution disclosure failures made the convictions unsafe
Compatibility of ex parte PII procedures with Article 6
Whether the court should consider additional grounds beyond the prosecution concession

notes: County court tax enforcement appeal; exclusive statutory appeal route and s70 certificates clearly upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Tax debt enforcement: county court bound by Commissioners' determination
key_facts: Mr Ahluwalia faced amended income tax and NIC assessments for 1991/92 to 1996/97 following a Revenue inquiry.
Accountant Neil Macpherson negotiated with the Revenue and the General Commissioners confirmed figures of about £160,000 on 26 May 2000 without attendance by Ahluwalia or Macpherson.
The Revenue obtained default county court judgment in January 2001 relying on section 70 certificates and later served a statutory demand.
Ahluwalia argued Macpherson lacked authority to agree figures and that no valid determination had occurred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from Reading County Court dismissing appeal against default judgment for tax arrears.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the county court had no jurisdiction to reopen the General Commissioners' determination and was bound by the section 70 certificates.
enrichment.ratio: The statutory machinery for appealing tax assessments through the General Commissioners is exclusive; their confirmation of agreed figures is a final determination under section 46(2), and section 70 certificates provide sufficient evidence in county court enforcement proceedings even where the taxpayer disputes an accountant's authority.
legal_issues: Whether county court may challenge a General Commissioners' tax determination
Effect of section 70 Taxes Management Act 1970 certificates in enforcement
Whether confirmation of agreed figures amounts to a determination
Authority of a taxpayer's accountant to bind the client

notes: Long commercial trial on exclusivity agreement and loss-of-chance causation; liability partly resolved at trial.

enrichment.short_title: Property exclusivity agreement: no loss of chance to buy Sandbrook Park
key_facts: Dandara agreed a seven-week exclusivity lock-out with CRS to buy Sandbrook Park headquarters in Rochdale for £15.25 million subject to contract.
During exclusivity Airtours viewed the property and offered £16 million; CWS, after merger, decided to remarket and sold to Airtours for £17.8 million.
Dandara claimed breaches caused loss of the chance to complete the purchase at the agreed price and sought an indemnity for due diligence costs.
Simon J had already held March negotiations breached clause 2.5; the trial focused on February breaches and causation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial on remaining liability and quantum after partial summary judgment on exclusivity breaches and indemnity.
enrichment.outcome: February breach of clause 2.4 (supplying sales brochure) did not cause loss; CWS would have remarketed even without the Airtours offer; further indemnity of £502.77 awarded under clause 7.
enrichment.ratio: A minimal February breach did not cause the loss of a real or substantial chance to buy at the heads-of-terms price because CWS had already decided before the Airtours offer to abandon the Dandara sale and remarket; mentioning an exclusivity agreement was not a breach of clause 6 confidentiality.
legal_issues: Whether February breaches caused Airtours' offer and loss of chance to complete
Construction of exclusivity clauses 2.4, 2.5 and 6
Whether deferred completion and Atos issues would have prevented exchange
Scope of clause 7 indemnity for due diligence costs

notes: Reflective loss preliminary issue on assigned company claim; Johnson/Giles/Shaker principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Reflective loss bars shareholder's assigned claim against director
key_facts: Mr Parker owned 85% of BDC; 15% was held in trusts for Mr Gardner's family.
BDC held 9% of Scoutvale and was owed £799,000; Parker allegedly caused Scoutvale to transfer Old Hall shares worth about £5m to Bweralley for £400,000 deferred.
BDC's liquidator assigned all rights of action to Gardner, who sued Parker for about £1.249m fiduciary breach losses.
Scoutvale's s423 proceedings against Bweralley were settled in 1995 releasing Parker except from liquidator claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from preliminary issue trial finding reflective loss barred recovery on pleaded case.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Gardner's assigned claim for diminution in Scoutvale share value and loss on the loan is barred by the rule against reflective loss.
enrichment.ratio: Losses suffered by BDC as Scoutvale shareholder and creditor merely reflect Scoutvale's loss recoverable from Parker; the rule applies to fiduciary claims and creditor claims alike and is not displaced by the 1995 settlement absent evidence Parker disabled Scoutvale from suing within the Giles exception.
legal_issues: Whether reflective loss applies to a claim for breach of fiduciary duty
Whether the Giles exception applies after the 1995 settlement
Whether creditor loss on an inter-company loan is reflective loss
Effect of assignment from a company in liquidation

notes: Permission to appeal refused on charging order/s423 findings; factual challenge on son's evidence held not arguable.

enrichment.short_title: Charging order upheld on assets transferred to defeat foreign judgment
key_facts: Habib Bank registered a Karachi High Court judgment for several million pounds against Mian Aftab Ahmed in England.
Ahmed's wife and sons claimed beneficial interests in the Watermead Hotel and Harper's Fitness Club through declarations of trust and gifts after proceedings began.
Simon J made absolute a charging order nisi and restored assets under section 423 as transactions to put property beyond creditors' reach.
Interveners sought permission to appeal relying on overlooked evidence from son Qamar about a 1994 conversation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against absolute charging order and section 423 restoration orders.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; Qamar's 1994 conversation evidence could not overcome the judge's findings that Pioneer dividends did not fund Mrs Ahmed's alleged contribution.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge has comprehensively rejected the source of purchase funds as incredible, a more credible recollection by one family member of being told the same story in 1994 does not create an arguable appeal; section 423 restoration following a registered foreign judgment stands.
legal_issues: Whether Qamar Ahmed's overlooked evidence could alter findings on asset ownership
Burden of proof on charging order and section 423 applications
Whether hotel and fitness club transfers were transactions defrauding creditors

notes: Special removal under Licensing Act 1964 s15; imminence and relevant date issues clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Special licence removal refused where CPO not yet imminent
key_facts: Ultimate Leisure sought to remove an on-licence from Mims Bar to the Gresham Hotel in Newcastle for a 420-capacity pub with music.
Local residents and trade objectors opposed the application; a compulsory purchase order affecting Mims was made but not confirmed when the special removal was applied for in March 2003.
Mims closed and its licence was suspended under section 141 after the CPO was made.
Licensing justices granted special removal in December 2003; Lightman J quashed the decision and remitted it.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review quashing grant of special removal under section 15 Licensing Act 1964.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; decision quashed outright rather than remitted because the March 2003 application was incompetent as Mims was not about to be pulled down or occupied for a public purpose.
enrichment.ratio: Section 15 requires practical certainty and imminence at the date of application; a CPO made but unconfirmed with completion targeted for 2005 does not satisfy 'about to be pulled down or occupied', and mere public ownership of vacant premises is not occupation for a public purpose.
legal_issues: When conditions for special removal must be satisfied
Meaning of 'about to be pulled down or occupied for a public purpose'
Whether adjourned licensing sessions reset the application date
Effect of section 141 suspension certificate
